Dear Diary, 2 December.
Exam in six days. Today I finally told Madhuri I haven't understood organic chemistry since the first unit. She stared at me. "Since July? Pooja, why didn't you say?" Because she's the smart one, and I didn't want her to know. Because every week I thought I'd catch up alone. Because it was embarrassing.
She sat with me for two hours. We did one chapter. There are seven. She was kind, but I could see her calculating how impossible it is. I felt so ashamed I wanted to disappear.
If I'd said something in July, it would have been one chapter at a time.
Pooja

qa.q: How did Uday feel after the manager was upset?
qa.a: Uday felt set up to fail and discouraged, since the manager had never said what was wanted.

qa.q: What could Uday do next time a task is unclear?
qa.a: Ask three questions before starting: why, by when and what good looks like, rather than guessing or freezing.

qa.q: How does Tanvir see the manager's criticism?
qa.a: Tanvir sees it as unfair, because the manager never gave the needed context.

grounding: A chat shows a junior given a task with no context or standard, guessing, and feeling set up to fail when criticised.

passage: Ira, twenty-three, had just started as an assistant at a small tourism office in Hampi. On Friday her boss, Vaibhav, handed her a folder. "Make something for the new visitors." He left for Bengaluru. Ira didn't know if he meant a brochure, a map or a website page; whether it was urgent; or who the visitors were. She chose a brochure and spent the weekend on it. On Monday he flipped through it and frowned. "I meant a one-page map for the hotel desks. This is too long." Ira's cheeks burned. That evening she wrote a list of questions to ask before starting any task. The next week, when he gave her a task, she asked all of them first, a little stiffly.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav say he meant after seeing the brochure?
qa.a: He meant a one-page map for the hotel desks.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when Vaibhav frowned at the brochure?
qa.a: Her cheeks burned; she felt embarrassed and unfairly judged, since she had been given no details.

qa.q: What did Ira do next, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She wrote a list of questions to ask before any task, which gets the context and standard up front.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Ira's new habit of asking questions?
qa.a: Vaibhav might find it a little stiff at first, but it will save him from wasted work and disappointment.

grounding: Shows a junior given a vague task who guesses, is criticised, and becomes more cautious.

passage: Hana had been at the marketing agency in Seoul for two months when her team leader, Chen, messaged: "Please handle the client's social media this week." No priority, no tone, no examples. Hana checked old posts, guessed a friendly style and posted twice a day. On Friday Chen called her in. "The client wanted formal posts. And only three this week." Hana nodded, heart pounding, and apologised. She didn't point out that nobody had told her. The next week, when Chen gave her another task, she hesitated for so long before starting that she missed the first deadline. Being wrong once had made her afraid to move at all.

qa.q: How many posts did the client want that week?
qa.a: The client wanted only three this week.

qa.q: How did Hana feel on Friday when Chen called her in?
qa.a: Hana felt anxious, with her heart pounding, and blamed herself though she hadn't been told.

qa.q: What would have helped Hana at the start?
qa.a: Chen stating the priority, tone and number of posts, or Hana asking about them before posting.

qa.q: How might Chen see Hana's hesitation the next week?
qa.a: Chen might see it as slowness, not realising that the unclear first task and criticism made Hana cautious.

grounding: Shows a junior given a task without priority or standard, criticised afterwards, and becoming more hesitant.

passage: Paulo had been made team lead at a design studio in Lisbon. He gave Esther, a talented junior, the task of designing a café menu. Then he checked in at ten, at noon, at three. Each time he suggested a change. On Friday she sent the final version. That night, alone in the office, Paulo moved the logo, changed two fonts and rewrote the headings. He sent his version to the client. On Monday, Esther saw it and went very quiet. The next task he gave her, she did exactly what he said, nothing more, and asked him about every small choice. Paulo felt uneasy. He had wanted her to own her work.

qa.q: What did Paulo ask Esther to design?
qa.a: A café menu.

qa.q: Why did Paulo keep checking in and rewriting the menu?
qa.a: He felt anxious about being accountable for the result, so he kept control of every detail.

qa.q: What could Paulo do differently next time?
qa.a: Agree one checkpoint and the quality expected, then let Esther deliver without quiet rewrites.

qa.q: How did Esther react to seeing her menu rewritten?
qa.a: Esther went quiet and stopped taking ownership, doing only what she was told and asking about every small choice.

grounding: Shows a lead who checks every step and quietly rewrites a junior's work, leading her to stop taking ownership.

passage: At the city school where Harsha was the new head of the science department, the annual science fair was his first big responsibility. He asked Santosh, an experienced teacher, to organise the student projects. Then he called Santosh every morning. He wanted copies of every plan. He re-did the layout of the hall without asking. The day before the fair, Santosh stopped replying to the group chat. When Harsha found him in the staffroom, Santosh said calmly, "If you want to do it yourself, tell me. I'll step back." Harsha felt his face go hot. He had been terrified of the principal's judgment, not of Santosh's skill. "I'm sorry. The fair's yours. I'll just come at the end."

qa.q: What did Harsha ask Santosh to organise?
qa.a: He asked Santosh to organise the student projects.

qa.q: What was Harsha afraid of behind the constant checking?
qa.a: He was terrified of the principal's judgment and anxious about being accountable for his first big event.

qa.q: What did Harsha do to repair things?
qa.a: He apologised, handed the fair back to Santosh, and chose to come only at the end.

qa.q: How did Santosh read Harsha's checking?
qa.a: Santosh read it as distrust and offered to step back, withdrawing from the group chat.

grounding: Shows a lead whose anxiety about accountability makes him check every step, which the teacher reads as distrust.

passage:
Dear Aparna,

I've been thinking about last month's report, and I owe you an honest note. When I gave you the donor section, I said it was yours. Then I asked for updates twice a day and rewrote your paragraphs at night without telling you. I told myself I was just polishing.

The truth is I was anxious. It was my first report as team lead, and if anything went wrong, it would be on my name.

I saw you stop suggesting ideas after the second week. I understand why. From now on: we'll agree what good looks like, meet once midway, and I won't touch your text without talking to you.

Jaya

qa.q: How often did Jaya ask Aparna for updates?
qa.a: Twice a day.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling while rewriting Aparna's paragraphs?
qa.a: Jaya felt anxious, worried that any mistake in the first report as team lead would be on Jaya's name.

qa.q: What does Jaya promise, and why could it rebuild trust?
qa.a: To agree what good looks like, meet once midway and not touch Aparna's text without talking, giving ownership back.

qa.q: How was Aparna affected by the micromanaging?
qa.a: Aparna stopped suggesting ideas after the second week, reading the checking and rewrites as distrust.

grounding: A lead's letter admits checking every step and rewriting a team member's work out of anxiety, and offers a fairer way.

passage: I sit across from Chaitanya at the architecture firm, so I heard how he handed Vinita her first solo project last week. He didn't just say "do the site plan". He said the client, a small school, needed a drawing for their funding application. He explained why it mattered: without it, the school couldn't apply this year. The deadline was the 20th, and it had to be neat enough for a government office, not a competition. Then he said, "Let's look at a rough version on Tuesday. How you draw it is up to you." Vinita asked two questions and got started. On Tuesday her draft was already close. I can't know what she felt, but she looked quietly proud walking back to her desk.

qa.q: Who was the client for Vinita's site plan?
qa.a: The client was a small school.

qa.q: What might Vinita have felt walking back from the Tuesday check?
qa.a: She looked quietly proud, likely feeling trusted and confident after her draft was already close.

qa.q: Which parts of Chaitanya's handover made it work?
qa.a: He gave the goal, why it mattered, the deadline, the quality expected and one checkpoint, then let Vinita choose her method.

qa.q: How does the colleague who sits across from Chaitanya see the handover?
qa.a: The colleague sees it as unusually clear and respectful, noticing both the details given and the freedom left to Vinita.

grounding: An observer describes a lead delegating with goal, reason, deadline, standard and one checkpoint, while leaving the method free.

passage:
Monday. Harsha, twenty-six, managed the front desk at a busy hotel in Jaipur. He asked Sumit, a new staff member, to prepare the welcome kits for a wedding group of eighty guests. He explained: the group arrives Thursday, the kits make the first impression, each needs a map, a schedule and a water bottle, and they should look neat, not fancy. "Show me three finished kits on Tuesday evening. After that, your way."
Tuesday. Sumit showed three kits. One map was folded wrong. Harsha pointed it out and left.
Thursday. Eighty kits lined the desk, with a small handwritten note in each that Sumit had added himself. The guests loved the notes. Harsha hadn't thought of that.

qa.q: How many guests were in the wedding group?
qa.a: There were eighty guests.

qa.q: What might Sumit have felt when he added the handwritten notes?
qa.a: He likely felt trusted and confident enough to add his own idea, since the method was left to him.

qa.q: Which parts of Harsha's delegation helped?
qa.a: He explained the goal, why it mattered, the deadline, the quality expected and a Tuesday checkpoint, then stepped back.

qa.q: How does Harsha feel when the guests love the notes?
qa.a: Harsha is pleasantly surprised and likely proud, seeing that giving freedom produced an idea he hadn't thought of.

grounding: Shows over several days a manager delegating with purpose, deadline, standard and one checkpoint, leaving the method to the staff member.

passage: Joseph, you asked how I learned to lead. Sit down. I'm Dolma, and when I was twenty-five I ran the weaving centre in our town near Darjeeling. My first big order was two hundred shawls for a shop in Delhi. I was so frightened I wanted to weave them all myself. My old teacher said, "Give it to your weavers, but tell them everything." So I did. I told Pema and the others the buyer, why the order could save the centre, the date the truck would come, and exactly how tight the weave should be. Then I said, "We'll check the first ten together. After that, weave your way." The truck left on time.

qa.q: How many shawls were in the order?
qa.a: The order was two hundred shawls.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel when the big order came?
qa.a: Dolma felt frightened, wanting to weave all the shawls alone rather than hand them over.

qa.q: Which choice in the story led to the truck leaving on time?
qa.a: Telling the weavers the buyer, the reason, the date and the standard, checking the first ten together, then letting them weave their own way.

qa.q: How might Pema and the other weavers have felt about the order?
qa.a: They likely felt trusted and responsible, knowing why the order mattered and being free to weave their own way after the check.

grounding: An elder recalls delegating a big order with goal, reason, deadline, standard and one check, then trusting the weavers' methods.
